items.prompt: A reporting job must read objects only under `reports/finance/` in one S3 bucket. Which policy change best applies least privilege while preserving the required access?
constraints: The job uses an IAM role rather than an IAM user.
The job must not read objects under other prefixes in the bucket.
The job needs `s3:GetObject` but does not need to list the bucket.

options.text: Allow `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/reports/finance/*` and do not grant unrelated bucket actions.
Allow `s3:*` on `arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/*` so future reporting changes will not require a policy update.
Allow `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket` because the bucket ARN automatically covers every object.
Allow `s3:ListAllMyBuckets` and rely on the application to avoid opening other prefixes.

feedback.Reason: Least privilege narrows both the action and the resource to the job's actual need.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: S3 object actions use object ARNs, and the object key prefix can be represented in the resource ARN. Granting a broader action set or relying on application behavior expands the authorization surface.
Details.scenarioApplication: The role can read only objects whose keys begin with `reports/finance/`, and no bucket-list permission is needed for the stated operation.
Details.errorCorrection: A bucket ARN is not a substitute for the object ARN required by `s3:GetObject`, and broad S3 permissions are not justified by possible future work.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The policy may need a separate, narrowly scoped `s3:ListBucket` statement if the job later needs prefix listing; that is a new requirement rather than a reason to pre-grant it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The wildcard action and whole-bucket object scope grant substantially more than the reporting job needs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: `s3:GetObject` targets objects, so the object ARN pattern is required; the bucket ARN alone does not represent every object.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Application discipline is not an authorization boundary, and listing all buckets is unrelated to reading one finance prefix.

items.prompt: An analyst must inspect the configuration of one DynamoDB table but must not read or write table data. Which permission set is the narrowest fit?
constraints: The analyst needs metadata such as table status and key schema.
The analyst must not call `GetItem`, `PutItem`, `UpdateItem`, or `DeleteItem`.
No other DynamoDB tables need to be inspected.

options.text: Allow the required `DescribeTable` action on the specific table ARN and omit data-plane actions.
Attach the AWS managed policy for full DynamoDB access because metadata is part of DynamoDB.
Allow all DynamoDB actions on `*` and depend on the analyst not selecting data operations.
Grant only `dynamodb:ListTables` on `*` because it automatically permits describing one table.

feedback.Reason: Least privilege distinguishes the required metadata action from data-plane actions and scopes it to the one table.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM policies grant named API actions and can scope resource-level actions to an ARN when the service supports that resource type. A list action is not an implicit allow for a describe action.
Details.scenarioApplication: The analyst needs table metadata only, so `DescribeTable` on the target table is the smallest stated permission.
Details.errorCorrection: A service-wide managed policy or wildcard action set would authorize data operations that the analyst does not need.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the analyst must discover the table name dynamically, a separately justified list permission may be needed, but it still would not replace `DescribeTable`.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Full DynamoDB access includes data mutations and reads beyond the metadata requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The wildcard action set is the opposite of least privilege and does not constrain the analyst's data access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: `ListTables` enumerates tables; it does not grant `DescribeTable` on the target table.

items.prompt: A support role may stop and start instances only when the instances carry the tag `Environment=Test`. Which policy design best narrows that authority?
constraints: The role must not stop or start production instances.
The team can require the tag on every managed test instance.
The same role may manage instances in more than one Availability Zone.

options.text: Allow the required EC2 actions with a tag-based condition that requires `Environment=Test` on the target resource.
Allow `ec2:*` on all resources because the tag is visible in the console.
Allow the actions only for one Availability Zone because an Availability Zone is the security boundary.
Use an application naming convention without a policy condition and review CloudTrail later.

feedback.Reason: A condition key can make the resource tag an authorization requirement instead of relying on operator intent or console visibility.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM condition elements can constrain an allow statement using request or resource context, including supported EC2 resource-tag condition keys. The condition is evaluated as part of authorization.
Details.scenarioApplication: The support role can perform only the specified lifecycle actions when the target instance has the required test tag, independent of Availability Zone.
Details.errorCorrection: A naming convention, console display, or later audit does not prevent an unauthorized stop or start operation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The tag becomes part of the security control and must be protected from unauthorized changes; tag-on-create controls may be needed in a complete design.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Wildcard EC2 permissions on all resources grant production authority and do not use the stated tag boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Availability Zone placement is not equivalent to the business tag boundary and would also exclude valid test instances in other zones.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A naming convention and retrospective logging do not enforce the restriction at request time.

items.prompt: A team is replacing a broad read-only policy for an existing role. Which AWS capability can use CloudTrail activity to help generate a narrower policy based on actions the role actually used?
constraints: The role has been used by the workload in a test account.
CloudTrail activity covers the relevant test period.
The generated result will be reviewed before deployment.

options.text: IAM Access Analyzer policy generation based on logged activity, followed by human review and testing.
The account root user, because only root can infer the minimum required actions.
The AWS shared responsibility model, because it automatically rewrites identity policies.
An S3 bucket policy, because all IAM policies are converted from S3 resource policies.

feedback.Reason: IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from observed CloudTrail activity, providing evidence for reducing unused permissions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Policy generation uses activity logged by CloudTrail to identify actions used by a role or user during a selected period. The result is a starting point and does not prove that unobserved future actions are unnecessary.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team can generate a candidate policy in the test account, compare it with the workload contract, and validate it before replacing the broad policy.
Details.errorCorrection: No root privilege or resource policy converts a broad identity policy into least privilege automatically.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A quiet test period can omit infrequent but required operations, so generation must be combined with workload scenarios, review, and staged validation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Root access does not infer workload behavior or create a least-privilege policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The shared responsibility model explains control ownership; it does not generate IAM policies.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An S3 bucket policy is a resource policy for S3 and cannot rewrite arbitrary identity policies.

items.prompt: A Lambda function needs to write one DynamoDB table. Which credential design best supports least privilege and avoids long-term secrets in the function configuration?
constraints: The function runs entirely on AWS Lambda.
The function needs only the table write operations defined in its role policy.
The team wants credentials to be rotated by AWS rather than embedded in code.

options.text: Attach a narrowly scoped execution role to the function and let Lambda obtain temporary role credentials.
Create an IAM user, put its access key in an environment variable, and grant broad DynamoDB access.
Use the account root access key as an encrypted environment variable.
Place a static access key in the deployment package and rely on package encryption.

feedback.Reason: An AWS workload should use an IAM role and temporary credentials instead of long-term access keys embedded in code or configuration.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Lambda execution roles provide the function with temporary credentials through the AWS runtime. The role permissions policy can be limited to the table and actions required by the function.
Details.scenarioApplication: The function receives its role credentials without storing a user or root secret, and its authorization is limited to the required DynamoDB write surface.
Details.errorCorrection: Encryption around a long-term key does not change its lifetime or broad identity risk, and root credentials must not be used by workloads.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The execution role still needs monitoring and periodic permission review; temporary credentials reduce key distribution risk but do not remove authorization design work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A static IAM-user key creates a long-term secret and the broad permission violates least privilege.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root credentials are unrestricted and are not a workload credential mechanism.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A packaged access key remains a long-term secret that can leak through artifacts or runtime access.

items.prompt: An unavoidable legacy integration uses one IAM-user access key. The team has created a replacement key and deployed it successfully. What is the safest next lifecycle step?
constraints: The replacement key has passed an end-to-end test in production traffic.
The old key is still active.
The team can monitor for calls made with the old key before deletion.

options.text: Deactivate the old key, observe for missed callers, then delete it after the migration is confirmed.
Leave both keys active indefinitely so future rollback is always possible.
Delete the new key immediately and keep using the old key because it is already known to work.
Publish the old key in a shared configuration file so every team can find the migration credential.

feedback.Reason: A staged deactivate-observe-delete sequence limits the overlap window while providing a reversible check for missed callers.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM access-key lifecycle operations include active, inactive, and deleted states. Rotating a key requires updating consumers, verifying the replacement, deactivating the previous key, and deleting it once it is no longer needed.
Details.scenarioApplication: Because the replacement is tested, deactivating the old key exposes any un-migrated caller without leaving the old credential permanently usable; deletion follows after confirmation.
Details.errorCorrection: Indefinite dual-active keys preserve unnecessary exposure, while deleting the known-working replacement reverses the intended migration.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The observation window should match the workload's real invocation pattern; a rare scheduled caller may require waiting for its schedule before deletion.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Keeping both keys active indefinitely increases exposure and defeats credential rotation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting the new key discards the validated replacement and leaves the old credential in use.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Sharing a secret in a common file expands access and creates a new distribution risk.

items.prompt: A credential review finds an IAM user's access key has been inactive for 180 days and has no documented owner. Which action best reduces unnecessary credential exposure?
constraints: No production dependency has been found for the key.
The user account has another approved authentication path.
The team can preserve audit records without retaining the active credential.

options.text: Confirm the key is unused, deactivate it, then delete it according to the organization's retention and recovery procedure.
Reactivate the key periodically so it does not become stale.
Copy the key to a second IAM user as an archive before leaving both keys active.
Grant the user administrator permissions so the inactive key has a clear owner.

feedback.Reason: An unneeded long-term key should not remain active; confirmation, deactivation, and deletion reduce the credential's attack surface.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Access keys are long-term credentials and can be deactivated or deleted. Credential reviews should identify unused keys and remove them after confirming that no workload depends on them.
Details.scenarioApplication: The key has no dependency or owner, so the team can revoke it and retain only the audit evidence needed for the procedure.
Details.errorCorrection: Age is not a reason to reactivate or duplicate a credential, and permission breadth cannot compensate for missing ownership.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deletion is harder to reverse than deactivation, so the team should follow its documented recovery window and verify dependencies before the final delete.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Reactivating an unused credential increases risk and does not address its lack of business need.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Duplicating a secret multiplies exposure and leaves both credentials active.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Administrator access is unrelated to credential ownership and would magnify the impact of compromise.

items.prompt: A security team needs a periodic account-wide inventory of IAM users, password status, MFA status, and access-key age. Which AWS capability best provides that snapshot?
constraints: The team needs identity credential metadata rather than application data.
The review covers IAM users in one AWS account.
The result will feed a human-reviewed remediation process.

options.text: Generate an IAM credential report and review its fields for stale or noncompliant credentials.
Use an EC2 instance status check because it reports all IAM user credentials.
Use an S3 inventory report because IAM passwords are stored as S3 objects.
Ask the root user to email each user's access key age to the security team.

feedback.Reason: The IAM credential report is designed to provide account-level credential metadata for IAM users.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An IAM credential report includes information about IAM user credentials such as console password presence, password age, MFA status, and access-key activity or age fields. It supports review rather than automatic authorization decisions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team can generate the report on a schedule, identify exceptions, and route remediation through an accountable process.
Details.errorCorrection: EC2 status and S3 inventory describe different resources, and root-user communication is not a credential-inventory mechanism.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The report is a point-in-time account view; it must be combined with ownership records and operational checks for complete lifecycle governance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: EC2 status checks report instance health, not IAM user credential posture.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 inventory concerns objects in S3 and does not contain IAM password or key metadata.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The root user does not provide a safe or scalable mechanism for collecting other users' credential metadata.

items.prompt: A company allows a small set of IAM users to use the AWS Management Console. Which control should the architect require for those human identities?
constraints: The users are not yet using a centralized workforce federation service.
The users' permissions remain limited to their job functions.
The company wants an additional factor at console sign-in.

options.text: Require a distinct MFA device for each IAM user and enforce the company's process for replacing or revoking lost devices.
Require users to share one MFA device so the account has only one registration.
Disable MFA because least-privilege policies already prevent credential theft.
Give every user the root user's MFA device so all console sessions use the same factor.

feedback.Reason: MFA adds an independent authentication factor for human console access and should be attributable to the individual identity.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM supports MFA devices for IAM users, and the device must be registered and managed as part of the user's authentication lifecycle. MFA strengthens authentication; it does not replace authorization policies.
Details.scenarioApplication: Each console identity has its own MFA enrollment and recovery process, so a stolen password alone is insufficient for sign-in.
Details.errorCorrection: A shared device destroys individual attribution and recovery control, while least privilege cannot prevent use of a stolen valid password by itself.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: MFA device loss and replacement must be planned; if the organization adopts federation, the workforce identity provider becomes the appropriate central MFA boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A shared factor weakens attribution and creates a common recovery and possession risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Least privilege limits actions after authentication; it does not provide a second factor or prevent password use.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The root MFA device belongs to the root identity and must not be shared with IAM users.

items.prompt: An IAM user may change its own console password and MFA device, but only after authenticating with MFA. Which policy mechanism best expresses that requirement for API requests?
constraints: The user has a long-term access key for an unavoidable legacy tool.
The sensitive self-service actions must require an MFA-authenticated request.
The policy should not grant the user permission to bypass the MFA condition.

options.text: Put the sensitive IAM actions in an allow statement conditioned on `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` being true.
Put the actions in an unconditional allow and ask the tool to include an MFA code in its user agent string.
Require the IAM user's access key ID to contain the letters `MFA`.
Attach the actions to the root user because root is the only identity that can use MFA.

feedback.Reason: The MFA context condition lets IAM authorize sensitive actions only when the request includes the required MFA authentication context.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` global condition key can be used in an IAM policy to require MFA for supported requests. The condition is evaluated by AWS authorization, not by a caller-controlled string.
Details.scenarioApplication: The user can perform the self-service changes only from a request whose authentication context satisfies the MFA condition, while the user keeps its narrow action set.
Details.errorCorrection: An unconditional allow and caller-supplied metadata do not create a trusted MFA requirement, and root is not a substitute for the user's policy.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The exact behavior depends on how credentials are obtained and which operations are covered, so the policy should be tested for both MFA and non-MFA request paths before rollout.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A user-agent string is caller-controlled and is not AWS's authenticated MFA context.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An access-key identifier has no semantic guarantee that MFA was used.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IAM users can use MFA, and moving actions to root would violate separation and root-safeguard principles.

items.prompt: A policy denies all actions unless `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` is true. A workload using an IAM role suddenly loses access because the role session does not include that condition key in the expected way. What is the safest design conclusion?
constraints: The workload uses temporary credentials from an IAM role.
The role is intended for machine-to-machine access rather than a human console session.
The team can separate human and workload authorization paths.

options.text: Do not apply a human MFA requirement indiscriminately to the workload role; separate human MFA controls from the workload's role trust and permissions design.
Give the workload the root MFA code on every request so all machine calls satisfy the human condition.
Disable the workload role and use a shared IAM-user access key because access keys always satisfy MFA.
Make the deny conditional on the application name supplied in the user agent so the workload can bypass it.

feedback.Reason: MFA conditions are appropriate for the authentication context they are intended to protect; forcing a human factor onto a machine role is a category error.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS global condition keys have credential-type and request-context behavior that must be understood before applying them. Human MFA authorization and workload role authorization should be modeled as distinct paths when their actors and credential flows differ.
Details.scenarioApplication: The workload keeps a role with least-privilege permissions and an appropriate trust policy, while human identities use MFA-protected access for their own sensitive operations.
Details.errorCorrection: Root MFA codes are not machine credentials, access keys do not inherently prove MFA, and caller-controlled user-agent data is not an authentication boundary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A separate control may be needed if humans can assume the workload role; that control should be attached to the human assumption path without breaking the workload's automated path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Root MFA is for root authentication and cannot be safely supplied to an automated workload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Replacing a role with an IAM-user key increases long-term credential exposure and does not make MFA automatic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An application name or user-agent value is caller-controlled and cannot substitute for an authenticated MFA context.

items.prompt: A human administrator may assume a high-privilege role only after using MFA. Where should the architect enforce that requirement?
constraints: The administrators authenticate as IAM users in the same account.
The target role is used for privileged changes.
The role should remain usable by an approved automation principal that does not use human MFA.

options.text: Require MFA in the trust policy for the human IAM-user principal path, while keeping a separate narrowly scoped trust path for approved automation.
Require the human to type an MFA code into the role's permissions policy because permissions policies control authentication.
Put the MFA requirement only in the administrator's local shell profile so AWS does not need to evaluate it.
Give the human root credentials because root MFA is stronger than role-assumption controls.

feedback.Reason: The role trust policy controls who may assume the role and can require MFA for the human principal path without imposing a human factor on approved automation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM role trust policies can use conditions such as `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` for a principal that assumes the role. The resulting role permissions policy controls actions after assumption; the two stages should remain distinct.
Details.scenarioApplication: Human administrators must present MFA before the high-privilege role is issued, while the automation principal uses its own explicit trust path with limited scope.
Details.errorCorrection: A permissions policy cannot authenticate a caller, and local shell settings are not an AWS-enforced control. Root use would weaken the design.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Separate trust statements must be reviewed carefully so the automation path cannot be used by an unapproved human principal and the human path cannot bypass MFA.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Permissions policies authorize actions after assumption; they do not establish the MFA requirement for assuming the role.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A local shell profile is not an authoritative AWS authorization control and can be bypassed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Root credentials are not required for role administration and should not be distributed to administrators.

items.prompt: An administrator performs routine log review and occasional production changes. Which identity design best reduces the blast radius of a compromised daily session?
constraints: Routine log review does not require production mutation permissions.
Production changes can be performed through an explicitly approved role.
Both paths need individual attribution and MFA for human access.

options.text: Use a lower-privilege daily identity and require a separate MFA-protected role assumption for production changes.
Give the daily identity administrator access so the administrator never has to switch identities.
Use the root user for log review and production changes because it has one audit trail.
Share one administrator access key among the operations team to simplify rotation.

feedback.Reason: Separating routine and privileged paths limits the permissions exposed during ordinary work and creates an explicit elevation step.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Least privilege is applied to the identity and session actually used for each task. A role can provide scoped, temporary privilege for a change without making that privilege available in every daily session.
Details.scenarioApplication: The administrator reviews logs with the daily identity and assumes the privileged role only for approved production changes after MFA.
Details.errorCorrection: Convenience-based administrator access and shared keys increase blast radius and reduce individual accountability; root is not a daily operator identity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The elevation workflow must be usable and auditable, with role permissions and trust reviewed independently; otherwise operators may create unsafe workarounds.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Permanent administrator access exposes production mutation authority during routine work and violates least privilege.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root use for daily operations is specifically unsafe and makes routine activity harder to constrain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Shared long-term credentials prevent reliable attribution and multiply the impact of a leak.

items.prompt: A team wants to replace an IAM policy with a narrower one after observing no denied requests for 30 days. What additional evidence is most important before removing permissions?
constraints: The workload has monthly and incident-driven paths that may not have run during the observation window.
The policy is attached to a production role.
The team can test representative workflows in a nonproduction environment before rollout.

options.text: Compare the proposed policy with all documented workload paths and test scheduled, recovery, and operational workflows before deployment.
Remove every action that did not appear in the last 30 days because absence of use proves it is unnecessary.
Replace the policy with administrator access during the test so no workflow can fail.
Ignore workload documentation because CloudTrail records every future action before it happens.

feedback.Reason: Observed activity informs least-privilege work but cannot prove that infrequent, recovery, or future-required operations are unnecessary.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Policy analysis based on activity is evidence from a time window. Least privilege still requires understanding the workload's complete operational contract and validating the replacement before production rollout.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team preserves actions required by scheduled jobs and recovery procedures, tests them in a representative environment, and then stages the narrower policy.
Details.errorCorrection: No activity in a short window is not proof of irrelevance, and temporary administrator access hides policy defects instead of validating the intended permissions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keeping an unneeded permission carries risk, but removing a recovery permission without a tested replacement can create an outage; the decision must consider both failure modes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A 30-day absence can miss monthly or incident-only paths and is insufficient by itself to prove the permission is unnecessary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Administrator access defeats the purpose of testing the proposed least-privilege boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudTrail records observed events; it cannot predict or authorize future workload operations.
